To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
progesterone is hydroxylated at the 7 beta,11 alpha and 15 beta sites by Aspergillus funigatus.

the filamentous fungus, A. fumigatus efficiently hydroxylates the steroid hormone progesterone, using two different cytochrome P-450 enzymes, one of which is inhibited by the azole antifungal, ketoconazole.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of microbial enzymes involved in the transformation of steroids and other biologically active compounds.
the identification of fungal cytochrome P-450 monooxygenases and their role in the biosynthesis of steroidal metabolites.
the identification of the sites of hydroxylation of steroids by fungi and bacteria, the enzymes responsible for these transformations and the mechanism of action of these enzymes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fungus A. fumigatus hydroxylates progesterone by a cytochrome P-450 dependent mechanism.
progesterone hydroxylation by A. fumigatus is a non-inducible, NADPH-dependent, microsome-mediated reaction, catalysed by at least two cytochrome P-450 monooxygenases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the filamentous fungus, A. fumigatus is a good model system for the study of cytochrome-P450 mediated steroid hydroxylation.
A. fumigatus possesses a cytochrome P-450 monooxygenase system which hydroxylates progesterone and other steroid substrates at the 11 alpha,15 beta and 7 beta sites.

the use of a combination of whole cell, microsomal and cytochrome P-450 reconstitution assays can be used to characterize and quantify the number and selectivity of cytochrome-P-450 enzymes involved in the metabolism of steroid substrates.
